facts.fact: Described by Gerald R. Allen and N. J. Cross in 1980.
It was one of the new rainbowfishes Allen described from Marinus Boeseman's 1954–55 collections from Netherlands New Guinea (West Papua).
The name joins Greek 'pseudo' (false) with G. incisa: the fish resembles its close relative and lives near it, but the likeness is a false one.
FishBase and the Catalog of Fishes spell the name Glossolepis pseudoincisa.
Wikipedia says the correct form, pseudoincisa, is almost always misspelt as pseudoincisus.
The genus Glossolepis belongs to the rainbowfish family Melanotaeniidae.
Listed as Vulnerable (B1ab(iii)) on the IUCN Red List, assessed on 5 December 2019.
Hobbyists often mistake it for its close relative Glossolepis incisus.
Compared with G. incisus, it is smaller and deeper-bodied, much redder (especially as an adult), and has more pointed dorsal and anal fins.
It is smaller and more compact than G. incisus, with more intense red colour and more pronounced fin markings and fin shape.
Its pectoral fins are uniformly pale and its pelvic fins mostly pale, while G. incisus has dusky fins.
Its scales are smaller than those of G. incisus and are aligned differently.
It has 38–43 vertical scale rows, 12–16 horizontal scale rows and 26–32 gill rakers on the first arch.
The dorsal fins have 6–7 spines and 10–12 soft rays, and the anal fin has 1 spine and 18–22 soft rays.
Maximum recorded size is 8.0 cm standard length.
Endemic to the Indonesian province of Papua (West Papua) on New Guinea.
The holotype comes from an isolated oxbow lake by the Tami River, about 23 km southeast of Jayapura. FishBase says the species is known only from that single 1954 collection.
The first specimens were collected by Boeseman in November 1954 in a Tami River oxbow lake about 30 km east of Lake Sentani.
Also reported from Lake Ifaten, Lake Iwom and Lake Yaniruk.
Another ANGFA page reports it from Lake Emfote, Lake Iwom and Lake Yaniruk.
The video says it lives in a handful of isolated lakes and calls the country Papua New Guinea. The scientific sources place it in Indonesian Papua.
A freshwater, benthopelagic fish of the tropics, at about 3–4°S.
Lake Ifaten is an isolated crater lake about 250 m across, in the mountains near Lake Sentani at about 300 m above sea level.
Lake Ifaten water measured about 28°C at pH 9.0.
It is kept in the aquarium hobby and sold by tropical fish dealers.
Its small range makes it vulnerable in the wild.
It looks dull in dealer tanks and needs a few months in a large aquarium, with good food, clean water and rival males, to colour up.
Fish from Lake Ifaten start colouring at about three months and reach full colour at about four months. G. incisus takes nearly a year.
The keeper wants a tank with a 4-foot (about 120 cm) footprint and recommends a 55-gallon tank, though the internet often suggests 40 gallons.
It looks best over dark substrate with a dark background, with plenty of open swimming lanes. Planted tanks suit it best, and blue backgrounds should be avoided.
Forgiving of water conditions: 72–79°F (about 22–26°C) and pH about 6.5–8.
It prefers somewhat hard water and copes with neutral water, but very soft water should be avoided.
It takes pellets, flake, frozen and live foods. A varied diet is best.
It has a narrow throat, so feed only very small pellets, because large ones can lodge and kill the fish.
Peaceful, active and constantly displaying. A shoaling fish best kept in groups of six or more.
Several males can live together. They spar with flaring, fin displays and short chases, but do no damage.
It often bumps into hardscape, which causes mouth marks that look like fungus. These clear up with clean water.
Suitable tank mates include other rainbowfish, corydoras, tetras, barbs, loaches, Geophagus and dwarf cichlids, but not very large fish.
Females are smaller than males and, unusually for rainbowfish, are also colourful.
Females reach about 6 cm total length and have horizontal zigzag yellow stripes on the body.
Females have a zigzagging yellow-and-red striped pattern.
Males have a criss-cross pattern of red lines on the gill cover, clearest at about one year old.
In aquaria it lays eggs on spawning mops or plants. The mops can be removed after about a week.
In aquaria the eggs hatch in under 7 days. After the first couple of days the tiny fry take baby brine shrimp.
Considered easy to breed in the aquarium.
